implementation_notes: Swift deliberately has no blocking queue - the concurrency model is async/await plus structured concurrency - so the hand-off is an AsyncStream: the producer pushes with continuation.yield(_:) from any concurrent context, the consumer drains with for await ... in, and the bufferingPolicy (bufferingNewest(n)/bufferingOldest(n)) is the buffer bound, because the default policy buffers without limit (Int.max). Production ends with continuation.finish(), which terminates the for-await loop after the remaining buffer is consumed, and cancellation propagates through onTermination; use a TaskGroup when several consumers should share the work. Keep blocking primitives (DispatchSemaphore.wait) off the cooperative pool, and use actors to serialize any shared state around the stream.
pitfalls: The default buffering policy is unbounded: without bufferingNewest/bufferingOldest the producer never backpressures and memory grows; the dropping policies instead discard elements, which must be acceptable.
Forgetting cont.finish() leaves for await waiting forever; finish also flushes the remaining buffer to the consumer.
yield is non-blocking and callable from any context, so producers must not assume the consumer has caught up - and isolation must be respected (hop to an actor or MainActor as needed).
Calling DispatchSemaphore.wait() on a cooperative-pool thread starves the pool; bridge legacy callbacks with continuations instead.

variants.name: Legacy libdispatch bounded queue (two semaphores + buffer)
variants.implementation_notes: Before Swift concurrency, the hand-rolled realization paired a lock (or serial DispatchQueue) guarding an array with two DispatchSemaphore values - one counting free slots and one counting items - so a producer waits on slots and signals items, and the consumer does the inverse: Dijkstra's two-semaphore buffer expressed with libdispatch. It still exists in legacy code and in code that must support pre-5.5 runtimes, but it blocks a thread on every wait and has no cancellation integration, so new code should use AsyncStream or actors instead.
pitfalls: Semaphore waits block a DispatchQueue thread, so more consumers than queue threads makes libdispatch spawn threads and hide oversubscription.
The buffer still needs its own lock (or serial queue): the semaphores count capacity but do not make array access atomic.
There is no cancellation: a thread parked in semaphore.wait() cannot observe Task cancellation - use wait(timeout:) when shutdown must interrupt it.
